docs.title: About
docs.text:
I'm Kamran, based in London. I moved into security from compliance work and I'm aiming for a SOC analyst role.

For three years I handled confidential immigration casework in regulated UK environments: more than 200 cases with zero refusals, under Home Office rules that kept changing. I guided students through university admissions and visa applications, and I set up an AI agent that sorted our enquiry forms and drafted replies for me to check. Before that I ran two branches of a language school with over 30 staff.

All of that meant working to procedure, keeping careful records and noticing when something didn't add up, which is a lot of what SOC work involves.

docs.title: Detections
docs.text:
Searches I have saved as alerts in my lab Splunk. For each one I write down what it catches, what it misses and how far I have tested it. They run on my home lab data (Windows Security log from one Windows 11 VM in index=main), so the index names and thresholds would need tuning anywhere else.

Rule Event Built Tested against Seen firing as a live alert Password guessing on one account 4625 28 Oct 2026 28 Oct and 6 Nov exercises Yes, 2 Nov 2026 Account lockout 4740 28 Oct 2026 28 Oct and 6 Nov exercises Yes, 2 Nov 2026

Both fired live for the first time on 2 November, when I re-ran the attack and watched them appear in Triggered Alerts.

One thing needed fixing. Each alert fired three times for a single attack. The rule runs every 5 minutes but looks back over the last 15, so the same failed logins were counted in three overlapping runs, and each run crossed the threshold. The logic was right. The schedule was double-counting. I added a 15 minute throttle, so once an alert fires it stays quiet for 15 minutes instead of re-firing on events it has already reported. I re-tested on 6 November and got one entry per rule.

Figure 1. 6 November: one spray, one Triggered Alerts entry per rule.

docs.title: Password guessing on one account
docs.text:
index=main EventCode=4625
| bucket _time span=5m
| stats count by Account_Name, _time
| where NOT like(Account_Name,"%$")
| where count>=5
| sort - count
  • What it does: counts failed logons per account in 5 minute buckets and keeps any account with 5 or more.
  • Schedule: every 5 minutes (cron */5 * * * *), searching the last 15 minutes. Triggers when there is at least one result. Action: Add to Triggered Alerts.
  • Why 5: the lockout policy on the VM locks an account at 10 failures. A threshold of 5 warns while the guessing is still going on, not only after the lock.
  • Why the $ filter: a 4625 holds two account names, the computer account that handled the request and the account that failed. Account_Name is a multivalue field, so stats splits each event into one row per name. Computer account names end in $, and the filter drops those rows. It has to come after stats, where each row holds a single name.
  • Watch out for: span=5 without the m means 5 seconds, and the rule would never fire on this data.
  • Catches: many wrong passwords against one account in a short time, for example the 10 failures in about 18 seconds on 28 Oct.

Figure 2. 6 November: the rule's own search during the spray. Each account went over the threshold of 5.

  • Misses: password spraying, where one password is tried across many accounts. Each account stays under 5. It also misses slow guessing spread out so that no 5 minute bucket reaches 5, and a burst that is split across two buckets (for example 3 in one and 3 in the next).
  • Likely false positives: a user who has forgotten a password and keeps retrying, or a service or saved session still using an old password.

docs.title: Account lockout
docs.text:
index=main EventCode=4740
  • What it does: fires on any account lockout.
  • Schedule: same as above, every 5 minutes over the last 15 minutes. Action: Add to Triggered Alerts.
  • Why a separate rule: a lockout is rare and worth a look on its own. It is logged as Audit Success, not Audit Failure, so a rule that only looks at failed audits would never see it.
  • Misses: anything that stays under the lockout threshold, including spraying.

Figure 3. 6 November: four lockouts, one for each account in the spray.

  • Note: for a local account the 4740 often leaves the caller computer name blank, as it did here. In a domain, the domain controller's 4740 should name the source machine.

docs.title: Still to build
docs.text:
• Password spraying: many different accounts failing from one source address in a short window. Pivot on the source, not the account.

On 6 November I ran a spray against four accounts at once. The password guessing rule above did fire, but only because my test put about 10 failures on each account, well over the threshold of 5. A real spray tries roughly one password per account, stays under the threshold, and would slip past this rule. So this still needs its own detection: count the distinct accounts failing from one source address over a longer window, not the failures per account.

docs.title: Topology
docs.text:
All the lab VMs share one VirtualBox Internal Network behind pfSense, separate from my home network.

Component Role Status VirtualBox Hypervisor Running pfSense CE Firewall, router and DHCP for the lab LAN Running Kali Linux Attacker box for generating test activity Running Metasploitable2 Deliberately vulnerable target Running Windows 11 + Sysmon Endpoint telemetry Running Ubuntu + Splunk SIEM Running Windows Server (AD DS) Domain controller on its own segment Planned

I picked Splunk over Security Onion because Security Onion needs about 16 GB of RAM, which doesn't fit in 32 GB alongside an AD lab.

Publishing rule

Write-ups never include real public IPs, passwords, API keys or anything from outside the lab.

docs.title: Hunting in BOTS v1: from a scanner to a quieter second source
docs.text:
Period covered: 3 and 5 November 2026 Dataset: Splunk "Boss of the SOC" v1 (BOTS v1), stream:http sourcetype Tools: Splunk Enterprise 10.4.1 Status: two sources investigated. What the second source's agent.php traffic really is stays unproven (see What I could not prove).

This is practice on a public training dataset, not a real incident. The page is about the method I used, so it does not give the answers to the dataset's questions. I have also left out every public IP address, because I do not publish them, even from a training set. In the searches they appear as <scanner> and <second_source>.

docs.title: How I worked
docs.text:
This is the order I actually followed, taken from my lab log.

  1. Choose the data and the target. The question was about a web scan, so I used stream:http, the sourcetype that records web requests. Then I found the busiest destination before looking at any source.
  2. Find who talks to it. Counting source and destination pairs gave me the scanner, and a much quieter second source.
  3. Split the second source by page. It only touched two pages.
  4. Split again by method and status. This gave me the counts I later checked.
  5. Read the full events. The raw requests and replies showed what was being sent and what came back.
  6. Chase the counts that did not add up. Two totals were each one higher than their groups, and finding the missing events led to the next step.
  7. Look at the User-Agents. One of the missing events had an odd browser string, so I counted them all.
  8. Compare the replies. I looked at what the server sent back and how often.
  9. Check outside sources. I searched for the file name to see if it belongs in a normal install.
  10. Separate what is proven from what is only supported or unproven.

I have not built a proper timeline yet. I only read times off tables, and that is the first job for next time.

docs.title: Part 1: finding the scanner (3 November)
docs.text:
The dest_ip field panel for all stream:http events put one internal address on top, with 22,643 of the 39,010 events. That was a strong sign it was the web server, but only a guess at that point.

Figure 1. The busiest destination in the web traffic. I cropped the list to the top row, because the rest are public addresses.

Next I paired every source with every destination:

index=botsv1 sourcetype=stream:http
| stats count by src_ip, dest_ip
| sort - count

One source sent 20,996 requests to the web server. The next sent 1,430.

Figure 2. Who talks to the web server most. I covered the two public source addresses with labels.

Being busy does not make a source a scanner, so I read inside its requests. One event put the site's name next to the web server's address, which confirmed what the server was. The same event had a request header in which the scanning tool named its own product. A second clue in the URLs it requested matched that product name, so two separate pieces of evidence agreed. Finally, a referrer filter showed that every one of those requests that had a src_ip came from the same address.

One thing is still open from this part. That referrer search returned 11,921 events, but only 11,918 had a src_ip. I have not looked at the other 3 yet.

docs.title: Part 2: the quieter second source (5 November)
docs.text: The second source was easy to skip: 1,430 requests against more than 20,000 from the scanner. I wanted to know what it was doing.

docs.title: Two pages, two jobs
docs.text:
src_ip=<second_source> dest_ip=192.168.250.70

The uri_path field had only two values:

Page Requests /joomla/administrator/index.php (the admin login) 1,236 /joomla/agent.php 194

Splitting by method and status gave three groups:

Figure 3. stats count by http_method uri_path status.

docs.title: The admin page: reading the events
docs.text:
I read the POST requests in full. All of them used the User-Agent Python-urllib/2.7, which is a script, not a browser. Each one sent the username admin with a different password. The pages that came back afterwards said "Username and password do not match". That is automated password guessing on the admin login.

I nearly made a mistake here. Every login POST got status 303, a redirect, and I first read 303 as "failed". Joomla redirects after every login attempt, whether it works or not. The warning text on the next page is the real evidence of failure.

docs.title: Counts that did not add up
docs.text:
The two groups were each one short. There were 412 POSTs, but only 411 had status 303. There were 194 requests to agent.php, but only 193 had status 200.

My first idea was to filter for the odd one out with status!=303, status=500 and status=200. All three returned nothing. That taught me that != skips events that have no status field at all. A missing value is not a different value.

So I paged through a table of the POSTs instead, and found the extra one on page 8:

Figure 4. The one POST with no status.

Its fields showed the request was captured but the reply was not (data_packets_out 0, missing_packets_out 1). It was a gap in the capture, so 411 plus 1 is 412.

I found the missing agent.php request the same way, at 22:56:18. Again no reply was captured, so 193 plus 1 is 194.

docs.title: How the gap led to the User-Agents
docs.text:
That missing agent.php request claimed to be Opera 9.52 on Windows. Earlier I had seen an agent.php request that claimed to be Safari on a Mac. One source should not be two browsers, so I counted the User-Agents for everything this source sent:

src_ip=<second_source> | stats count by uri_path http_user_agent

Figure 5. The admin page only ever saw one User-Agent. agent.php saw a different one almost every time.

The admin page had one row: Python, 1,236. Taking that away from the 1,430 total leaves 194, which is every agent.php request. Those 194 used 182 different browser strings: Chrome, Firefox, Safari, Opera and Internet Explorer, on Windows, Linux, Mac, iPhone and iPad. Most appeared once.

A tool rotates its User-Agent like this to get past blocklists, to beat simple "one User-Agent, many requests" rules, and to look like many visitors. It did not hide the one thing that gave it away: every request still came from the same address.

docs.title: What agent.php sent back
docs.text:
uri_path="/joomla/agent.php"
| stats dc(http_user_agent) as UA_Count dc(dest_content) as Response_Count

Figure 6. 182 User-Agents, 17 different replies.

A normal web page comes back as HTML. These replies were one made-up tag around text that looks like base64:

Figure 7. The 17 different replies, all in the same made-up tag.

Only 51 of the 194 requests got any reply content in the capture. The same short reply came back 34 times, one came back twice, and 15 were each unique. The other 143 had no captured reply content. Reading the table, the requests came in quick bursts of about 4 to 9 inside a second or two, usually with one reply per burst. I saw that in the timestamps; I did not measure it with a search.

Last, I searched for the file name. As far as I could find, agent.php is not part of a standard Joomla install. I have not checked that against an official Joomla file list.

docs.title: Proven
docs.text:
These come straight from searches and screenshots.

  • One quiet source sent 1,430 requests to the web server, to two pages only.
  • 1,236 went to the admin login, all with Python-urllib/2.7, sending the username admin with changing passwords. The pages after showed "Username and password do not match".
  • 194 went to agent.php, all to the same web server, using 182 different User-Agents.
  • No browser User-Agent ever hit the admin page, and Python never hit agent.php.
  • 143 of the 194 agent.php requests had no captured reply content. There were 17 different replies. The most common appeared 34 times.
  • Every agent.php reply with content (all 51) used the same made-up tag around base64-looking text.
  • Both off-by-one counts were capture gaps: the request was recorded and the reply was not.
  • != and stats both skip events where the field is missing.

docs.title: Supported, not proven
docs.text:
The evidence backs these, but they are conclusions, not facts.

  • The admin traffic was automated password guessing. This one is very strong.
  • agent.php traffic is software talking to software, not a person browsing.
  • The User-Agent rotation was meant to avoid detection.
  • The requests came in bursts. I saw this in the table but did not measure it.

docs.title: What I could not prove
docs.text:
• Whether agent.php is a backdoor or web shell.
  • Whether the encoded replies are harmful, or contain commands.
  • Whether anyone logged in to the admin page successfully. I read some of the 824 admin page replies, not all of them.
  • Whether the attacker uploaded agent.php, or whether the password guessing led to it.
  • Whether agent.php existed before 22:55, or whether any other source used it.
  • Whether the second source is the same attacker as the scanner. Nothing links the two addresses yet.

The timing suggests a story. The password guessing was running until at least 22:46, and agent.php traffic starts at 22:55. One possibility is that the attacker guessed the admin password, used the admin panel to plant agent.php, then started using it. To prove it I would need a successful login and a file upload or edit before 22:55.

docs.title: Next steps
docs.text:
1. Build the timeline properly: first and last time for each page.
  2. Read all 824 admin page replies for a successful login.
  3. Decode one short reply and see whether it is readable or still scrambled.
  4. Check whether any other source ever requested agent.php.
  5. Look at the 3 events with no src_ip from Part 1.

docs.title: What I learned
docs.text:
• Splitting one source by what it touches showed it was doing two different jobs.
  • When a total is off by one, go and find the missing event. Here the search for one missing event led straight to the User-Agent rotation.
  • Counting distinct values with dc() exposed the rotation, which raw counts would have hidden.
  • I keep facts, conclusions and guesses in separate lists, because a conclusion can sound like a fact once it is written down.

docs.title: Building an isolated home lab with pfSense and Kali
docs.text:
Built: mid-2026 SY0-701 domains: 3 (Security Architecture), 4 (Security Operations) Tools: pfSense CE 2.8.1, VirtualBox, Kali Linux

This is the first stage of my home lab: a pfSense firewall in front of an internal VirtualBox network, with Kali as the first machine on it. I built it on my Windows PC while studying for CompTIA A+, Network+ and Security+ and working through TryHackMe.

Where I relied on pfSense's defaults or haven't built something yet, I say so.

docs.title: Scope
docs.text: The lab is one LAN segment behind pfSense. pfSense handles routing and DHCP for it, and I manage it over HTTPS. Kali is on the network and can reach the internet. The point is isolation, keeping lab traffic away from my home network, so there is one WAN and one LAN and no second segment. What I haven't done is listed under Limitations and Next steps.

docs.title: Goal
docs.text:
I wanted somewhere to practise attacking, and later defending: running scans, starting deliberately vulnerable machines and eventually monitoring the traffic, without any of it landing on my home network.

The part of the design that does this is VirtualBox's Internal Network. An internal network is a virtual switch with no connection to the host's network card or my home LAN. The lab VMs can talk to each other and to pfSense, and the only way out is through pfSense's WAN interface.

That boundary works in one direction for now. Nothing on my home network can start a connection into the lab, because pfSense's WAN side blocks unsolicited inbound traffic. Going the other way, the default LAN rule allows traffic to any destination, and VirtualBox NAT sits behind the WAN, so a lab VM could probably still reach devices on my home network. Blocking that is on the list below.

docs.title: Architecture
docs.text:
[Internet]
     |
[pfSense WAN  em0]  DHCP client -> 10.0.2.15/24   (VirtualBox NAT)
     |
[pfSense LAN  em1]  static 192.168.1.1/24, DHCP server (.100-.200)
     |
  intnet  (VirtualBox Internal Network)
     |
[Kali Linux]  192.168.1.101 (DHCP)
Interface VirtualBox adapter Addressing Role WAN (em0) NAT DHCP client, 10.0.2.15/24 Route out to the internet through VirtualBox NAT LAN (em1) Internal Network intnet Static 192.168.1.1/24, DHCP pool .100 to .200 Gateway and DHCP for the lab

A VM joins the lab by setting its own adapter to the same internal network name, intnet. pfSense's one LAN adapter serves the whole virtual switch, so I don't need a new pfSense interface for each machine. Kali was the first. Metasploitable2, an Ubuntu VM running Splunk and a Windows 11 endpoint have joined the same LAN since.

10.0.2.15/24 is VirtualBox's default NAT range, so it's a private address. Nothing here shows a real public IP, my home router's address or a MAC address.

docs.title: pfSense VM
docs.text: Setting Value Version CE 2.8.1 (the current stable release when I installed it) RAM 1024 MB vCPUs 2 Disk 20 GB Guest OS type FreeBSD (64-bit), set by hand because VirtualBox didn't detect it Firmware EFI off

docs.title: Build steps
docs.text:
1. Installed pfSense CE from the AMD64 ISO. WAN came up as em0 on DHCP. I kept the default ZFS/GPT layout and chose Install CE instead of the paid Plus path ("Retry Validation").
  2. Got stuck in a boot loop on the first reboot and fixed it (see Other problems).
  3. Added a second VirtualBox adapter on Internal Network intnet, which became the LAN.
  4. In the pfSense console, used Assign Interfaces to set WAN = em0 and LAN = em1.
  5. Gave LAN a static 192.168.1.1/24 with no upstream gateway. Only WAN needs one.
  6. Turned on the DHCP server for LAN with a pool of 192.168.1.100 to 192.168.1.200.
  7. Kept the web GUI on HTTPS when the console offered to switch it to HTTP.
  8. Moved Kali onto intnet, brought its interface up with DHCP, and then ran into the DNS problem below.

docs.title: Firewall rules
docs.text:
I'm running pfSense's default rules. I didn't write them, but I can explain them:

  • On LAN, the default "allow LAN to any" rule lets the lab make outbound connections.
  • On WAN, all unsolicited inbound traffic is blocked, along with private and bogon source addresses. Nothing from the WAN side reaches the lab unless a rule allows it.

Anything the WAN side doesn't explicitly allow is dropped (implicit deny). I haven't written rules of my own or read the firewall logs yet. That is first on my list.

docs.title: DNS troubleshooting
docs.text:
Once Kali had a DHCP lease from pfSense, ping google.com failed:

ping: google.com: Temporary failure in name resolution

Before blaming the firewall or the internet connection, I pinged a raw IP to separate name resolution from connectivity:

$ ping 8.8.8.8
64 bytes from 8.8.8.8 ... 0% packet loss     # routing, NAT and internet fine
$ ping google.com
ping: google.com: Temporary failure in name resolution   # only DNS fails

The IP worked, so routing, NAT and the internet connection were fine and the problem had to be DNS. I pointed Kali at a nameserver by hand:

$ echo "nameserver 8.8.8.8" | sudo tee /etc/resolv.conf
$ ping google.com    # resolves now, ~20 ms replies, 0% loss

This is a workaround. /etc/resolv.conf is often managed automatically and can be overwritten by the next DHCP lease or a reboot. The lasting fix is to make sure pfSense includes a DNS server in its DHCP offer (Services > DHCP Server) so no one has to patch the file on each client.

The method is to test one layer at a time. If the IP works and the name doesn't, it's DNS, and there's no need to start pulling apart the firewall.

docs.title: Other problems
docs.text:
• Boot loop after install. The VM kept rebooting into the installer because the ISO was still attached and booted before the disk. I powered off, removed the ISO under Settings > Storage, and it booted the installed system. I now check this after every VM install.
  • No dhclient on Kali. sudo dhclient eth0 gave "command not found" on this image. sudo dhcpcd eth0 worked and pulled the lease (offered 192.168.1.101 from 192.168.1.1, default route via 192.168.1.1), which also confirmed pfSense was acting as DHCP server and gateway.
  • Kali's .vbox file didn't show in Import Appliance. The importer only lists .ova and .ovf files. Double-clicking the .vbox file opened it, and switching the file filter to "All files" would have worked too.
  • VirtualBox didn't recognise pfSense. I set the guest type to FreeBSD (64-bit) myself.

docs.title: What I learned, and the Security+ links
docs.text:
• Isolation. The Internal Network has no direct path to my home LAN, and the only way out is through pfSense. It's a small case of separating networks by trust level, although the lab is one flat segment inside.
  • Implicit deny. pfSense's WAN side drops any inbound traffic that no rule allows.
  • DHCP, DNS and the default gateway. I watched pfSense lease an address and set the default route, and I separated a DNS fault from a routing fault.
  • Secure defaults. I kept HTTPS on the management interface.

docs.title: Limitations
docs.text:
• One flat LAN, with no second segment or DMZ.
  • Default firewall rules only.
  • Lab VMs can probably reach my home network through the default LAN rule.
  • No testing between segments and no firewall log review yet.
  • No NTP at first, so clocks drifted across VMs. I fixed this later by making pfSense the lab's time source: see Can I trust the timestamps in my lab SIEM?.

docs.title: Next steps
docs.text:
• Add a second Internal Network behind a new pfSense interface (OPT1) and write rules for what can cross between the two segments. After that I'll be able to answer firewall rule questions from experience.
  • Add a LAN rule that blocks the lab from reaching my home network's address range, then confirm it from Kali.
  • Write explicit LAN and OPT1 rules, then check the firewall logs to see what they block.
  • Hand out DNS through pfSense's DHCP settings instead of editing /etc/resolv.conf.
  • Try Suricata or Snort on pfSense.
  • Done in October 2026: every VM now takes its time from pfSense (see the timestamps write-up).
  • Write up the later stages (Metasploitable2, the Windows 11 endpoint with Sysmon, and Splunk) as separate pages.

Environment: Oracle VirtualBox on Windows, i7-11800H with 32 GB RAM. All addresses shown are private lab ranges. I used Claude as a build partner and to talk through troubleshooting. I carried out and checked every step myself and can explain why I did each one.

docs.title: SMB password guessing: run it, find it, detect it
docs.text:
Period covered: 26 to 28 October 2026 SY0-701 domains: 4 (Security Operations) Tools: Splunk Enterprise 10.4.1, Windows Security auditing, Kali Linux Status: detection built, password spraying rule not built yet (see What this misses)

This is a lab exercise on my own network. I ran the attack myself against a Windows VM I own so I could learn to spot it from the defender side. Nothing here is a real incident, and this page has no passwords or attack steps. It is about the detection.

docs.title: The setup
docs.text:
• Target: a Windows 11 VM with a local account and file sharing over SMB (port 445).
  • Source: a Kali Linux VM on the same lab network.
  • Collection: a Splunk forwarder on the Windows VM sends the Security log to Splunk on Ubuntu.

SMB is the Windows file and printer sharing protocol. Password guessing over SMB means trying passwords against an account through that service until one works.

docs.title: What should happen, and what happened
docs.text:
When someone guesses passwords against a local account, Windows should record each failed attempt as event 4625 (an account failed to log on). My lockout policy locks an account after 10 bad tries. So I expected a run of 4625 events and then a lockout.

Figure 1. 27 October: the lockout policy on the Windows VM, checked the day before the test. The weak password rules (minimum length 0, no history) are lab settings, not a recommendation.

That is what I got. In Splunk:

What Event What it showed Failed logons 4625 10 failures on one account in about 18 seconds, roughly 2 seconds apart The lockout 4740 one event, right after the 10th failure A later allowed logon 4624 a successful network logon, but only after I unlocked the account by hand and used the correct password as part of the test

Figure 2. 28 October: the attack tool reported a timeout on every attempt. I cropped off the command and the password list above it.

Every 4625 showed the same three things: Logon Type 3 (a network logon, not someone at the keyboard), Sub Status 0xC000006A (the username was real and only the password was wrong), and the Kali VM as the source address.

Figure 3. 28 October: one of the 4625 events in Splunk, with the fields I used highlighted.

Figure 4. 28 October: the 4740 lockout, logged in the same second as the last 4625.

docs.title: What I checked
docs.text:
I went through the events with the questions a ticket would ask.

  • One account or many? One. That points to guessing against a single account, not password spraying.
  • Wrong password or wrong username? The 0xC000006A sub status says the username was valid, so whoever did this already knew a real account name.
  • At the keyboard or over the network? Logon Type 3 means another machine.
  • Did it work? Not in the attack run. The 10th failure locked the account first.
  • Did the attack tool tell the truth? No. It reported connection timeouts, but every attempt still showed up in Splunk. I trust the target's logs over the attacker's output now. I didn't expect to learn that one.

docs.title: The detection I built
docs.text:
I saved two searches as alerts in Splunk.

The first looks for the guessing pattern. It counts failed logons per account in five-minute buckets and flags any account with five or more:

index=main EventCode=4625
| bucket _time span=5m
| stats count by Account_Name, _time
| where NOT like(Account_Name,"%$")
| where count>=5
| sort - count

The NOT like(Account_Name,"%$") line drops computer accounts, whose names end in a dollar sign, so they can't trigger the alert on their own.

The second fires on the lockout itself:

index=main EventCode=4740

Figure 5. 28 October: both alerts saved and enabled in Splunk. The "Send email" action shown on the first one was removed later the same day; both now only add to Triggered Alerts.

Both alerts run every five minutes over the last 15 minutes. I checked the search logic against the events from this exercise, but I haven't yet watched either alert fire on its own. That test is next. More detail on each rule is on the Detections page, and the same incident written up as a ticket is HL-2026-1028-01.

docs.title: What this misses
docs.text: The first rule watches for many failures on one account. It would not catch password spraying, where one password is tried against many accounts. Each account stays under five failures, so the rule never fires. Catching that needs a different rule: many different accounts failing from one source address in a short window. I haven't built it yet.

docs.title: What I took from it
docs.text: Event 4625 tells you more than "someone typed a bad password." The logon type, the sub status and the source address together say what kind of attack it is and where it came from. I was also surprised that Windows logs the 4740 lockout as Audit Success, because the lockout action itself succeeded. And the attack tool's own output was wrong about what happened, while the logs on the target were right.

docs.title: Can I trust the timestamps in my lab SIEM?
docs.text: Period covered: 12 to 20 October 2026 SY0-701 domains: 4 (Security Operations) Tools: Splunk Enterprise 10.4.1, pfSense CE, Windows Time service, systemd-timesyncd Status: clock problem fixed, VM freezing still open (see Still open)

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: I loaded a 33-million-event dataset into Splunk and my searches kept dying. Raising the VM's memory did not fully fix it. The VM also stalled, and the timestamps in my own lab logs did not line up. I traced the timestamp problem to machines that did not share a clock, made my pfSense firewall the lab's time source, and checked the result. The clocks now agree to within milliseconds. The VM stalls are still unexplained.

docs.title: The lab
docs.text:
VM Role Address pfSense Firewall, DHCP, DNS, now NTP 192.168.1.1 Windows 11 evaluation Endpoint with Sysmon and the Splunk Universal Forwarder 192.168.1.104 Ubuntu 24.04 Splunk Enterprise 10.4.1 192.168.1.103

VirtualBox on a Windows laptop (i7-11800H, 32 GB). Kali and Metasploitable2 are in the lab too.

docs.title: How it started: searches that would not finish (12 October)
docs.text:
I loaded the public Splunk "Boss of the SOC" v1 dataset into its own index, botsv1. A raw search over all time kept ending with "Search auto-canceled".

Figure 1. 12 October: the first raw search over botsv1 ends in "Search auto-canceled".

My first theory was that the search was filling the disk. I tested it by running index=botsv1 earliest=0 | stats count, which writes almost nothing to disk. It was cancelled too, so the theory was wrong.

The Job Inspector gave the real picture. For the bare search, most of the time went to reading raw events, and it had read about 70,000 of 33,413,777 events (roughly 0.2%) before it was cancelled. My reading is that "auto-cancel" here is an inactivity timeout and not a runtime limit: the search crawled until it stopped reporting progress. The VM had 4 GB of RAM, and Splunk's health panel showed Resource Usage red. A tstats count returned the full 33,413,777 in about a second, because it reads the index files and not the raw events.

That evening I raised the VM to 8 GB and 4 vCPUs. free -h then showed 7.7 GiB and nproc showed 4.

Figure 2. 12 October: after the resize, free -h shows 7.7 GiB and nproc shows 4.

docs.title: It kept going wrong (13 to 16 October)
docs.text:
On 13 October the same raw search, index=botsv1 earliest=0 | stats count, was auto-cancelled again, now on the bigger VM. So more memory had not made raw searches work.

Figure 3. 13 October: the same raw search is auto-canceled again on the bigger VM.

On 16 October the Splunk VM's console printed kernel warnings: rcu_preempt detected stalls and "Possible timer handling issue on cpu=0".

Figure 4. 16 October: kernel warnings on the Splunk VM console.

Later that day I ran a lag check on my own lab data, the gap between when an event says it happened (_time) and when Splunk received it (_indextime):

index=main earliest=-15m
| eval lag=_indextime-_time
| stats avg(lag) max(lag) by source

Average lag was 254 s for Sysmon, 305 s for Security and 293 s for System, with maximums up to 408 s. That was my first observation: a large positive lag. Events appeared to arrive minutes after they happened. I did not compare the clocks that day, so I did not know why.

Figure 5. 16 October: the positive lag, average 254 to 305 seconds per source.

I had met clock trouble before. In August, searches on "last 15 minutes" had missed events, and I had used "All time" as a workaround and noted that the lab had no shared clock. It was still unfixed in October.

docs.title: Why timestamps matter
docs.text: An investigation reads events from several machines in order. If two clocks disagree, the order is wrong, and a command can look as though it ran before the login that caused it. Kerberos in Active Directory rejects logins when clocks differ by more than 5 minutes by default. And Splunk's time-range searches only work if the event's time is right.

docs.title: Following the clock (19 October)
docs.text:
I measured before changing anything.

  • pfSense ntpq -p: three working upstream servers agreeing at offsets of about -22 to -24 ms, plus a pool entry that was unreachable.
  • Win11 w32tm /stripchart /computer:192.168.1.1: about 2.7 s off pfSense, and w32tm /query /status showed its source as "Local CMOS Clock" and not synchronised.
  • Splunk VM timedatectl timesync-status: offset +547 ms, jitter 478.5 ms, frequency +500 ppm.

Figure 6. 19 October: pfSense's upstream time servers and their offsets. I masked the refid column and the two servers listed by IP address.

Figure 7. 19 October: Win11 sync status and stripchart beside the early lag search.

Then the lag, per event. I computed lag=_indextime-_time for each event and looked at the smallest value per source, not the largest. That was my second observation: every source showed a negative lag, roughly -34.6 s to +1.0 s. A negative lag means Splunk "received" an event before it says it happened, which cannot be true. It means the two clocks disagreed at that moment.

So these are two separate observations. On 16 October the lag was positive and large, 250 to 400 seconds. On 19 October it was negative and small, in seconds. I do not know that they share one cause. I could only tie the 19 October one to the clocks, because that is when I measured them.

docs.title: Wrong turns
docs.text:
• Maximums hid the problem. My first lag search used max(_time) and max(_indextime) per source. The gaps looked like small lags of 0 to 34 s. Only the per-event version showed the negative values.
  • A suggested install replaced my time service. ntpq told me to apt install ntpsec. I did, and it replaced systemd-timesyncd. I reinstalled systemd-timesyncd to put it back.
  • I blamed the freezing for the big lag numbers. Later, drilling into the biggest values showed they were something else (below).

docs.title: The fix
docs.text:
pfSense is the single time source. It has the internet connection and answers time requests from the LAN.

On the Splunk VM I created a drop-in file, /etc/systemd/timesyncd.conf.d/pfsense.conf, and restarted the service. The file contains:

[Time]
NTP=192.168.1.1

On Win11:

w32tm /config /manualpeerlist:192.168.1.1 /syncfromflags:manual /update
w32tm /resync /rediscover

The first /resync failed with "no time data was available". /resync /rediscover worked. After that, w32tm /query /status showed source 192.168.1.1, and the stripchart showed about -8 ms.

docs.title: Result (20 October)
docs.text:
On the Splunk VM, timedatectl timesync-status read: server 192.168.1.1, stratum 3, offset -717 us, jitter 668 us, delay 948 us, frequency -1.356 ppm.

Figure 8. 20 October: the Splunk VM syncing from pfSense, offset -717 us.

The per-source lag check, for events received in the last 15 minutes:

Source Events Min lag (s) Max lag (s) PowerShell 9 1.234 3.092 Sysmon 555 0.052 27.914 Security 256 0.342 43.723 System 92 0.813 54.249

Every minimum is positive. The negative lag is gone.

Figure 9. 20 October: per-source lag after the fix. Every minimum is positive.

The maximums are still tens of seconds. I opened the biggest ones. The largest System value, 54.248 s, covered seven events that all carried the same event time, 13:47:31.752, and were Windows kernel boot messages. The big Security and Sysmon values were events logged within about a minute of the same boot. That fits the forwarder's startup: it connects after boot, and events Windows logged before it connected arrive in one batch. It is not a clock error.

docs.title: Still open
docs.text:
• The Splunk VM still stalls. On 19 October the kernel logged a 162-second soft lockup, and on 20 October I caught one live: a 23-second lockup on CPU#0 and another on CPU#3 while a Splunk process was running. After the stall the clock was off by about 2 ms, so the clock now survives it, but the stalls are unexplained. I suspect something on the host, and I have not shown it.
  • Win11's Root Dispersion was 7.78 s on 20 October and I have not rechecked it.
  • Raw searches on the 8 GB VM were still being cancelled on 13 October. I have no clean explanation yet.
  • My early 19 October times are approximate.

docs.title: What I learned
docs.text:
• Per-event values show what maximums hide.
  • Read what apt wants to install before saying yes. It can replace the thing you are fixing.
  • Change one setting at a time, and write down what each change did.
  • A clean cause for one symptom (big lag from the forwarder's startup) does not explain another (the stalls).
  • Do not call something fixed until it has been checked again.

The screenshots above are cropped from my own lab consoles. Only private lab addresses appear; I masked the public IPs of upstream time servers in Figure 6.

I'll list rooms here as I finish them, with one thing I learned from each.

Note

docs.title: Ticket HL-2026-1028-01: SMB password guessing, account locked out
docs.text:
A practice ticket written from my own lab exercise, in the format I use for every finding. It is not a real incident. The full story with screenshots is in the write-up: SMB password guessing: run it, find it, detect it.

Field Value ID HL-2026-1028-01 Date 28 Oct 2026 Analyst Kamran Source Exercise. I ran the activity myself. No alert fired, because the alerts below were built from this work afterwards Severity Medium Verdict True positive (simulated) MITRE ATT&CK T1110 Brute Force, T1110.001 Password Guessing

docs.title: Host, user and IP
docs.text:
• Target: DESKTOP-7DMB70C (Windows 11), 192.168.1.104
  • Account targeted: analyst (local account)
  • Source of the attempts: 192.168.1.100 (the Kali VM)
  • Splunk indexer: 192.168.1.103

All addresses are on the private lab network behind pfSense.

docs.title: Severity and why
docs.text: Medium. One account took 10 failed network logons in about 18 seconds from one source, which is a clear guessing pattern. The account lockout policy stopped it at the 10th attempt, so no access was gained in this run. It is an attempted compromise that a control contained, not a breach.

docs.title: Evidence
docs.text:
• index=main EventCode=4625 (last 15 minutes): 10 failed logons on DESKTOP-7DMB70C between 12:06:23 and 12:06:41, roughly 2 seconds apart. Each one has Logon Type 3 (network), Sub Status 0xC000006A (valid user, wrong password), Source Network Address 192.168.1.100, and authentication package NTLM.
  • index=main EventCode=4740: one event at 12:06:41, account analyst locked out. It is logged as Audit Success, not Audit Failure.
  • Screenshots: figures 1 to 4 in the write-up (lockout policy, tool output, 4625, 4740).

docs.title: What I checked
docs.text:
• One account or many? One. That points to guessing against one account, not spraying.
  • Wrong password or wrong username? Sub Status 0xC000006A means the username was valid, so the source already knew a real account name.
  • At the keyboard or over the network? Logon Type 3 is a network logon from another machine.
  • Did it succeed? Not in this run. The 10th failure locked the account. Later I unlocked the account by hand and tested the correct password on purpose, which gave a successful network logon (4624, Type 3). That was part of the exercise, not a compromise.
  • Did the attack tool report success? No. It reported connection timeouts, yet every attempt reached Splunk. The logs on the target are the record to trust, not the tool's own output.

docs.title: Next step or escalation
docs.text: In a real environment I would confirm whether 192.168.1.100 is an authorised host, check where else analyst is used, and make sure SMB (TCP 445) is not reachable from general network segments. I would escalate to Tier 2 if the same source showed up against other accounts, because that would suggest spraying.

docs.title: Limits
docs.text: The detection behind this ticket (5 or more 4625 on one account in a 5 minute window) catches guessing against a single account. It misses password spraying, where one password is tried against many accounts, because each account stays under the threshold. That needs a separate rule: many different accounts failing from one source address. See Detections.

docs.title: Ticket HL-2026-1106-01: Password spraying, four accounts locked out
docs.text:
A practice ticket from my own lab exercise, in the format I use for every finding. It is not a real incident. It is the companion to my first ticket: that one was many passwords against one account, this one is a few passwords across four accounts. The detection results and screenshots are on the Detections page.

Field Value ID HL-2026-1106-01 Date 6 Nov 2026 Analyst Kamran Source Exercise. I ran the activity myself. Two saved Splunk alerts fired on it live Severity Medium Verdict True positive (simulated) MITRE ATT&CK T1110 Brute Force, T1110.003 Password Spraying

docs.title: Host, user and IP
docs.text:
• Target: DESKTOP-7DMB70C (Windows 11), 192.168.1.104
  • Accounts targeted: analyst, spraytest1, spraytest2, spraytest3 (local accounts)
  • Source of the attempts: 192.168.1.100 (the Kali VM)
  • Splunk indexer: 192.168.56.10

All addresses are on the private lab network behind pfSense.

docs.title: Severity and why
docs.text: Medium. Four accounts each took about 10 failed network logons from one source inside the same few-minute window, which is the shape of a password spray. The lockout policy caught every account at the threshold, so no access was gained. It is an attempted compromise that a control contained.

docs.title: Evidence
docs.text:
• index=main EventCode=4625 (last 24 hours): 40 failed logons on DESKTOP-7DMB70C. Each has Logon Type 3 (network), Error Code 0xC000006D (wrong user or password), Logon Process NtLmSsp, Source Network Address 192.168.1.100.
  • index=main EventCode=4625 | bucket _time span=5m | stats count by Account_Name _time | where NOT like(Account_Name,"%$") | where count>=5: analyst, spraytest1, spraytest2 and spraytest3 with 10 failures each, all in one 5-minute bucket.
  • index=main EventCode=4740: 4 lockout events, one per account.
  • Triggered Alerts: 2 entries, Brute force detection and Account Lockout (4740), one each. Screenshots are on the Detections page.

docs.title: What I checked
docs.text:
• One account or many? Four, each with about 10 failures from one source. That is spraying, not guessing against a single account.
  • Wrong password or wrong username? Error Code 0xC000006D, so the credentials failed.
  • At the keyboard or over the network? Logon Type 3, so network logons from another host.
  • Did it succeed? No. Every account locked at the threshold.
  • Why did only 10 of the 13 passwords show as 4625? After lockout the account is locked, so Windows stops checking the password. Later attempts log with the reason "account locked" (0xC0000234), not "bad password". The tool stopped after lockout, so those did not appear. I cannot claim the full list of passwords tried, only the ones that reached the password check.
  • Did the throttle fix hold? Yes. On 2 Nov each alert fired three times for one attack. After I added a 15-minute throttle, this run gave one entry per rule.

docs.title: Next step or escalation
docs.text: In a real environment I would confirm whether 192.168.1.100 is an authorised host, check where these accounts are used, and make sure SMB (TCP 445) is not reachable from general segments. I would escalate to Tier 2 if the same source hit more accounts, or if any account showed a successful logon (4624, Type 3) after the failures.

docs.title: Limits
docs.text: Both rules caught this because the lockout threshold is low. A slow spray, roughly one password per account spread over hours, would stay under the threshold and could slip past both. A low-and-slow rule needs a longer window and a count of distinct accounts per source address, not raw counts per account. See Detections.
